recall.a: Lee knew cheap flats were not the best economic choice. He wanted people with a weak national identity to have something to fight for. This shows his core logic: in a small, fragile country, every policy served survival, even when it meant heavy state control.

cards.title: Nietzsche: no one can build your bridge for you
cards.body: The young Nietzsche says finding yourself is not digging down. It is climbing up. List what you have truly loved, and the list becomes a ladder. Good teachers don't build you; they clear the weeds.

sections.text:
A hare has seven skins, Nietzsche writes. A person could peel off seventy times seven layers and still not be able to say: this one is the real me. He wrote this in 1873, when he was almost thirty, in an essay called Schopenhauer as Educator.

This is not the cold, sharp voice of our daily Beyond Good and Evil installment. It is the young, hopeful Nietzsche, writing about happiness and freedom. Here is the heart of the essay:

"No one can build you the bridge on which you, and only you, must cross the river of life."

"No one can build you the bridge." The key word is build. Others can give advice, but no one can do the work for you. Just before this line, he says that anyone who does not want to be one of the crowd need only stop making things easy for himself. The bridge is hard on purpose.

"You, and only you." One "you" would be enough. He says it twice to shut the door on excuses. In the next sentence he admits that ready-made bridges are everywhere. There are even demigods, or half-gods, who would gladly carry you across. But the price is pawning yourself. To pawn something is to hand it over for a loan, and often you never get it back.

"The river of life." You cross a river by moving. He never promises what waits on the other side. Where does the path lead? His answer: stop asking, and walk.

So how do you know which bridge is yours? Looking deep inside yourself is risky, he warns. You can give yourself wounds that no doctor can heal. So he offers a gentler method. Ask what you have truly loved so far. What has lifted your soul and delighted it at the same time? Put those things in a row. Together they may show a law, like the steps of a ladder you have been climbing. Then comes the twist. Your true self is not buried deep inside you. It stands high above the person you usually call "I".

This changes what teachers are for. Real culture, he says, does not hand you artificial limbs or a wax nose, fake parts stuck on from outside. Instead it pulls weeds, clears away rubble, and chases off the pests that attack young shoots. In his words, "your educators cannot go beyond being your liberators." A good teacher does not make you. They free what is already there, trapped and hard to reach.

He is honest about his limits. There may be other ways to wake up to yourself, he says. He just knows none better than thinking about the people who shaped you. Without this freedom, a person squints to the left, to the right, backwards, in every direction except their own. The cure is not more looking around. It is building your own crossing.

sections.label: See it in your life
items: Name three things that both lifted you and delighted you: a book, a person, a piece of work. Ask what they share.
Notice when you check left and right before a choice. Nietzsche calls that squinting.
Think of your best teacher. Did they add something to you, or clear something away?

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Your true self is not buried below you. It is the next step up the ladder of what you have loved.

recall.q: Where does Nietzsche say the true self is found, and what does that mean a good teacher can do?
recall.a: Not deep inside you, but high above you. List what you have truly loved, and the list forms a ladder you have been climbing. So a teacher cannot build a self for you. They can only free you, like pulling weeds away from a young plant.

cards.title: How fast you age in your 40s may predict memory slips later
cards.body: In a study of 232 adults, the ones whose bodies were aging faster in their 40s forgot more planned tasks about ten years later. Their biological age did not predict this. Only their speed of aging did.
cards.evidence: single study · n=232 · self-reported memory lapses · correlational

sections.text:
At ten at night, a pill is still sitting in its strip on the kitchen counter. You meant to take it at dinner. You didn't forget where the pill was. You forgot to do the thing you had planned.

Psychologists call this a prospective memory lapse, which means forgetting a future task. It is different from a retrospective lapse, where you forget something from the past, like where you put your keys. Researcher David Almeida says prospective lapses happen less often but can be more serious. Losing your keys is annoying. Missing medicine doses or doctor's visits can do real harm.

A team at Penn State wanted to know if the body's aging could predict these slips. In the 2000s, they took blood from 232 adults who were in their 40s. They tested the blood with three molecular clocks. These are tools that estimate how old your body is from chemical signs in your blood. Two clocks gave a biological age: how old the body seems, whatever the birthday says. The third clock, called DunedinPACE, measured something else: how fast the body is aging right now. It was built by following about 1,000 people since the 1970s and checking 19 signs of organ health every year.

Almeida uses a car to explain the difference. Most clocks are like an odometer. They show how far you have already gone. DunedinPACE is like a speedometer. It shows how fast you are going.

About ten years later, the researchers called the same people eight times. They asked how often each kind of memory lapse happened and how much it got in the way of daily life.

The odometers predicted nothing. Biological age did not match memory lapses at all. The speedometer did. People who were aging faster in midlife were 18 percent more likely to have a prospective lapse. The researchers say that could mean forgetting something on about five more days each month. Earlier research has linked frequent prospective lapses with dementia later in life, so these slips may be an early sign of it.

The researchers don't say anyone is doomed. They say midlife, a busy and stressful time, is when you should notice changes in your thinking and tell your doctor about them. Almeida points out that cognitive decline, meaning worse memory and thinking, has many physical causes, from poor blood flow to lack of sleep. Many of these causes can be treated, and catching them early could help for decades.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: This is one study of 232 people. It shows a link, not a cause: fast aging went with more memory slips, but the study cannot show that one caused the other. The lapses were self-reported, meaning people described their own memory over the phone. The dementia link comes from earlier research, not from this study.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: How far your body has come told the researchers nothing. How fast it was going told them something.

recall.q: Which measure of aging predicted memory lapses ten years later, and what kind of lapse was it?
recall.a: Only the pace of aging, measured by the DunedinPACE "speedometer" clock, predicted them. Biological age, the "odometer", did not. Faster agers were 18 percent more likely to have prospective lapses, meaning they forgot planned tasks like taking medicine.
